15885:
Ancient peoples around Israel worshipped the sun, the moon and the stars as gods: Shamash the sun god of justice in Mesopotamia, Sin the moon god of Harran and Ur, and the planets and constellations as divine beings who shaped fate. The Bible calls them 'the host of heaven'.

In Judah's last century this worship came right into the temple. Manasseh built altars for the host of heaven in its courts; there were horses dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance and 'chariots of the sun'; people burned incense on their rooftops to the stars. Josiah swept it all away, and Ezekiel still saw twenty-five men in the inner court bowing east to the sun with their backs to God's house.
15886: In Mesopotamia Shamash crossed the sky each day in his chariot and passed through the underworld at night, seeing everything; so he was the god of justice and oaths (he hands Hammurabi his laws on the famous stele). Sin the moon god kept time and gave omens. Babylonian astrology read the will of the gods in the stars. In Ugarit the sun was a goddess, Shapash, 'torch of the gods', who helps find the dead Baal. Judah stood between these worlds, and Assyrian domination in the 8th-7th centuries BC brought more astral religion with it, though how much was imposed and how much was local is debated.
15887:
Genesis deliberately calls the sun and moon just 'the greater light' and 'the lesser light', lamps God hung in the sky, perhaps to avoid names that were also gods' names (Gen 1:16; a common but debated reading). Deuteronomy warns Israel not to bow down to the sun, moon and stars, which God 'allotted to all the peoples' (Deut 4:19; Deut 17:3). Job protests that he never kissed his hand to the shining sun or moon (Job 31:26-28).

The northern kingdom worshipped the host of heaven (2 Kgs 17:16). Manasseh built altars for all the host of heaven in both temple courts (2 Kgs 21:3; 2 Kgs 21:5). Josiah removed the priests who burned incense 'to Baal, to the sun and the moon and the constellations and all the host of the heavens', took away the horses the kings had dedicated to the sun at the temple entrance, burned the chariots of the sun, and pulled down the rooftop altars of Ahaz (2 Kgs 23:4-5; 2 Kgs 23:11-12). Jeremiah and Zephaniah condemn rooftop offerings to the host of heaven (Jer 19:13; Zeph 1:5). Ezekiel sees about twenty-five men in the inner court facing east and bowing to the sun (Ezek 8:16).

At the same time the Bible uses solar language for God: 'the LORD God is a sun and shield' (Ps 84:11); 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings' (Mal 4:2). Some scholars (notably in the 1993 study *Yahweh and the Sun*) argue that some Judahites actually worshipped Yahweh in solar form, so the 'horses of the sun' were Yahweh's; others think they were for a separate sun god introduced under Assyrian influence. It is debated.

15912: After the exile, Jewish practice made a point of turning away from sun worship: the Mishnah (*Sukkah* 5:4) records that during the Feast of Tabernacles priests turned toward the temple and declared that their fathers had turned their backs on the temple and bowed east to the sun, 'but as for us, our eyes are to the LORD'. The Roman cult of Sol Invictus later became a major rival to early Christianity; early Christians themselves prayed facing east toward the rising sun as a symbol of Christ's return, while insisting they did not worship the sun (Tertullian answers this charge in *Apology* 16). Astrology, the heir of star worship, has never fully gone away.

15928: Marduk was the patron god of the city of Babylon and, from about 1100 BC onward, the head of the Babylonian gods. People usually called him simply Bel, meaning 'lord' (the same word as the Canaanite title Baal). When the prophets mock 'Bel' they are mocking the chief god of the empire that destroyed Jerusalem.
15929:
Marduk's great myth is the *Enuma Elish* ('When on high'), a Babylonian creation epic probably composed in the late second millennium BC and recited at the New Year (akitu) festival. In it the older gods are threatened by Tiamat, the salt-water sea pictured as a monstrous mother. The young Marduk agrees to fight her on condition that he is made king of the gods. He catches her in a net, drives a wind into her mouth, shoots an arrow through her, and splits her body in two like a dried fish, making the sky from one half and the earth from the other. He then creates humans from the blood of Tiamat's defeated general Qingu so that people can do the gods' work, and the gods build Babylon and the Esagila temple for him. The poem ends by listing his fifty names.

The story was political as well as religious: it explained why Babylon and its god stood at the top of the world. When Babylon rose, Marduk rose with it; earlier versions of the same kind of story gave the hero's role to other gods such as Enlil or Ninurta.
15930:
Marduk appears in the Bible mainly under his title Bel, and once as Merodach. Isaiah pictures the fall of Babylon as a humiliating removal van: 'Bel bows down, Nebo stoops' — the great statues that were carried in triumphant procession at the New Year festival now have to be loaded onto tired animals and carried into captivity themselves (Isa 46:1-2). The contrast is pointed: Babylon's gods must be carried, but Israel's God carries his people (Isa 46:3-4). Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon announces that 'Bel is put to shame, Merodach is dismayed' (Jer 50:2) and that God will punish Bel in Babylon and make him spit out what he swallowed (Jer 51:44).

His name also survives inside personal names: Merodach-baladan, the Babylonian king who sent envoys to Hezekiah (Isa 39:1), and Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk, 'man of Marduk'), who released King Jehoiachin from prison (2 Kgs 25:27). Daniel's Babylonian name Belteshazzar is said in the text to be 'according to the name of my god' (Dan 4:8); the Akkadian behind it is usually reconstructed as Balatsu-usur ('protect his life'), so the link to Bel may be a wordplay rather than a precise etymology.

Most striking of all, the Babylonian propaganda of Cyrus claimed that Marduk chose Cyrus to restore order, while Isaiah says it was Yahweh who called Cyrus 'his anointed' (Isa 45:1; Isa 44:28). Two theologies describe the same event, each crediting its own god.
15931: Bel and Nebo carried off on beasts of burden
15932: Isaiah turns the New Year procession upside down: the idols that were paraded through Babylon become baggage loaded onto weary animals. The point is that a god who has to be carried cannot carry anyone.
15933: Bel put to shame, Merodach shattered
15934: Jeremiah's long oracle against Babylon names its chief god directly and announces his humiliation alongside the fall of the city.
15935: Cyrus: chosen by Marduk or by Yahweh?
15936: When Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, his own cylinder inscription said Marduk had searched for a righteous king and chosen him. The biblical writers say Yahweh stirred Cyrus's spirit. Isaiah even adds 'though you do not know me' (Isa 45:4), conceding that Cyrus was not a worshipper of Israel's God.
15938: Merodach-baladan (Marduk-apla-iddina II) courted Hezekiah as an ally against Assyria; Evil-merodach freed Jehoiachin. Both names carry the god's name, a reminder of how much Babylonian public life was bound up with him.

15940: A clay barrel inscribed in Akkadian after Cyrus's capture of Babylon in 539 BC. It says Marduk grew angry with the last Babylonian king, Nabonidus, chose Cyrus, and let him enter Babylon without a battle; it also describes returning gods and peoples to their home sanctuaries. It does not mention the Jews, but historians widely see it as the same policy reflected in Ezra 1.
15942: Babylon (excavated by Robert Koldewey; reconstructed in Berlin)
15943: Glazed-brick walls show rows of mushhushshu dragons, Marduk's animal, along with bulls and lions. This was the road down which Marduk's statue travelled at the New Year festival — the very procession Isa 46 mocks.
15944: Etemenanki ziggurat and the 'Tower of Babel' stele
15946: The seven-stage temple tower beside Marduk's temple was rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II. A black stone stele in the Schøyen Collection shows Nebuchadnezzar beside the tower. Many scholars think towers like this lie in the background of the Babel story (Gen 11:1-9), though the Genesis narrative is set much earlier and the link is a matter of background, not identity.
15950: Copies of the creation epic invited comparison with Gen 1, especially the dividing of the waters. Most scholars now see Genesis as answering the same questions very differently — no battle, no divine bodies, humans made in God's image rather than as slave labour — rather than borrowing directly.
15952: Bel is not a disguise but the ordinary Akkadian title 'lord', cognate with Hebrew baal. Merodach is the Hebrew spelling of Marduk. Some scholars suggest the vowels of Merodach were shaped by the pattern of other deliberately altered names (like Molech), but there is no clear evidence of a shame-word here; it may simply reflect how the name was pronounced.
15953: Marduk's cult continued under the Persians and Greeks; Alexander the Great planned to rebuild the Esagila, and cuneiform temple records from Babylon run into the first century AD. As Babylon emptied, the god faded. In Jewish storytelling he survived as the idol unmasked by Daniel in the Greek addition *Bel and the Dragon*, where priests secretly eat the food offered to Bel. Some have suggested that the name Mordecai derives from Marduk; this is widely accepted as the etymology of the name but says nothing about Mordecai's own faith.
15964: A scribe's stylus or wedge, often shown standing on a mushhushshu dragon or on a clay tablet
15968: Nabu was the Babylonian god of writing and wisdom, the patron of scribes, and the son of Marduk. In the Bible he is called Nebo. His name is hidden in some of the most famous names of the exile: Nebuchadnezzar and Nebuzaradan both begin with 'Nabu'.
15969:
Nabu had few long stories of his own. His importance lay in his job: he was the divine scribe who wrote on the 'tablet of destinies', recording each person's fate and the lifespan of kings. In the first millennium BC he became so popular that Assyrian and Babylonian kings named their sons after him. An Assyrian inscription on a Nabu statue from Kalhu (Nimrud) reads, roughly, 'trust in Nabu, do not trust in any other god'.

Every year at the New Year festival Nabu's statue was carried by boat from his temple at Borsippa to Babylon to visit his father Marduk, and then carried home again. If the festival could not be held, as happened during King Nabonidus's long absence in Arabia, the chronicles note that 'Nabu did not come to Babylon'.
15970:
Isaiah names Nebo alongside Bel as the two great gods of Babylon who end up as cargo: 'Bel bows down, Nebo stoops' (Isa 46:1). The image almost certainly plays on the procession in which Nabu was ferried to Babylon each year.

Nabu also appears in personal names connected with Judah's fall: Nebuchadnezzar (Nabu-kudurri-usur, 'Nabu, protect my heir'), his captain Nebuzaradan (Nabu-zer-iddin, 'Nabu has given offspring', 2 Kgs 25:8), and the officials Samgar-nebo and Nebushasban (Jer 39:3; Jer 39:13). Many scholars think Abednego's name (Dan 1:7) is a deliberate distortion of Abed-nebo ('servant of Nabu'), changing the god's name so it could not be honoured; others see it simply as an Aramaic form. This is debated.

A separate question is whether the Moabite town and mountain called Nebo (Num 32:3; Deut 34:1) were named after the god. Some scholars think a West Semitic form of the deity lies behind the place name; others think it is an unrelated word. Treat it as debated.
15972: The idol of the scribe-god, who supposedly wrote the destinies of nations, cannot save itself from being carried away.
15974: The Babylonians who besieged and burned Jerusalem carried Nabu's name. Jeremiah lists several of the officials who sat in the city's Middle Gate after it fell.
15976: Azariah was renamed Abednego. If the original was Abed-nebo, the book of Daniel may have scrambled the god's name, much as other biblical writers changed Baal names. This is a reasonable but unproven suggestion.
15977: Mount Nebo and the town of Nebo
15978: Moses viewed the land from Mount Nebo. Num 32:38 notes that the Reubenites changed the names of some towns including Nebo, which may hint that the names had pagan associations. The Mesha Stele also mentions Mesha taking the town of Nebo from Israel.
15982: This chronicle records year after year that because the king stayed in Tayma (Arabia), 'Nabu did not come to Babylon, Bel did not come out' and the New Year festival was not held. It confirms how central the Nabu-and-Bel procession was to Babylonian religion — the procession Isa 46 turns into a joke.
15986: The ruined ziggurat of Borsippa, rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II, was long confused by travellers with the Tower of Babel. Inscribed cylinders of Nebuchadnezzar and Antiochus I describe rebuilding Nabu's temple.
15990: A small business tablet dated 595 BC names Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, a chief eunuch of Nebuchadnezzar. Many scholars connect him with 'Sarsechim, Rab-saris' in Jer 39:3, though the exact reading of the Hebrew name list is debated.
15992: One common suggestion is that a scribe changed b to g so that the name no longer honoured Nabu. Others think 'nego' is a genuine variant or an Aramaic form. The evidence is not decisive.
15993: Nabu was one of the last Mesopotamian gods to be worshipped. His cult spread to Syria, where he was honoured at Palmyra and Edessa into the Roman period, and Greek writers sometimes matched him with Apollo or Hermes as a god of learning. Borsippa's temple was still functioning in the Seleucid era.

16003: Enlil, chief god of Nippur (in most traditions)
16004: Nergal was the Mesopotamian god of plague, war and the land of the dead, and his chief city was Cuthah in central Iraq. When the Assyrians resettled people from Cuthah in the former kingdom of Israel, they brought Nergal with them. The Bible states this in a single sentence that matches the god to the right city.
16005:
In the myth *Nergal and Ereshkigal*, the gods hold a banquet and Ereshkigal, queen of the underworld, cannot come up to it, so she sends her messenger. Nergal fails to show proper respect and is summoned below. In one version he storms the underworld with demons and seizes the throne; in another, longer version he and Ereshkigal become lovers, and he ends up ruling the underworld with her. Either way, the story explains how a warrior god came to be king of the dead.

In the related *Erra Epic* (first millennium BC), the plague-and-war god Erra (identified with Nergal) persuades Marduk to leave his throne and then runs amok, devastating Babylon, until he is calmed. Copies of this poem were used as amulets against plague.
16006:
After Samaria fell (722 BC), the Assyrians deported many Israelites and brought in people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim (2 Kgs 17:24). Each group 'made its own gods': 'the men of Cuth made Nergal' (2 Kgs 17:30). The writer of Kings correctly pairs Cuthah with its patron god, which shows real knowledge of Mesopotamian religion.

The narrator's point is that these settlers 'feared the LORD and served their own gods' at the same time (2 Kgs 17:33; 2 Kgs 17:41) — a mixed religion. Later Jewish writers called the Samaritans 'Cutheans' (Kutim) after this verse, a hostile nickname implying that their worship was foreign in origin. Samaritans themselves reject that account of their origins.

Nergal's name also appears in Nergal-sharezer (Nergal-sharri-usur, 'Nergal, protect the king'), a Babylonian official present at the fall of Jerusalem (Jer 39:3; Jer 39:13). He is often identified with Neriglissar, who later became king of Babylon (560-556 BC); that identification is likely but not certain.

16008: Settlers in Samaria set up Nergal's image in the old high places while also hiring an Israelite priest to teach them how to 'fear the LORD'.

16014: Sargon II claims he deported about 27,000 people from Samaria and resettled the city with people from other conquered lands, matching the policy described in 2 Kgs 17:24.
16018: One of Sennacherib's city gates was named for Nergal and guarded by human-headed winged bulls. The bulls were badly damaged by militants in 2015.
16019: Nergal remained a feared god into Hellenistic and Parthian times; at Hatra and Palmyra he was matched with Heracles. Later Jewish tradition (b. Sanhedrin 63b) claimed the Cutheans' Nergal had the form of a rooster, a rabbinic guess based on a wordplay, not on Mesopotamian evidence. In medieval and early modern demonology Nergal became a minor demon, sometimes called a 'chief of secret police' in hell — a purely literary invention.

16040: Ishtar was the most important goddess of Mesopotamia: goddess of love, war and the morning and evening star (Venus). She is not named directly in the Bible, but many scholars think she stands behind the 'Queen of Heaven' whom the women of Judah honoured with cakes, and she is the lover of Tammuz, for whom women wept at the temple gate.
16041:
In the Sumerian *Descent of Inanna* (and the shorter Akkadian *Descent of Ishtar*), the goddess decides to visit the underworld, ruled by her sister. At each of seven gates she must give up one piece of clothing or jewellery, until she arrives naked and powerless and is struck dead and hung on a hook. With the help of the god of wisdom she is revived, but she may only leave if someone takes her place. She finds her lover Dumuzi enjoying himself instead of mourning, and hands him over to the demons. In a fragment published by Samuel Noah Kramer in 1963, Dumuzi's sister agrees to share his fate, so each spends half the year below.

Ishtar is also the dangerous goddess of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, who proposes to Gilgamesh; when he refuses, listing the bad ends of her earlier lovers, she sends the Bull of Heaven to punish him. She was the battle goddess of Assyrian kings, who claimed she marched before their armies.
16042:
No biblical verse names Ishtar outright, so every link is inferred.

1. **The Queen of Heaven.** Jeremiah condemns families who make cakes, pour drink offerings and burn incense to 'the Queen of Heaven' (Jer 7:18; Jer 44:17-19). Ishtar bore titles like 'Lady of Heaven', and cakes were offered to her in Mesopotamian ritual; but Astarte and Anat were also called 'queen of heaven' in Egyptian and Levantine sources. Most scholars think the Judahite goddess was a blend in which Ishtar's influence (spread by Assyrian domination) mixed with the local Astarte. See the separate entry queen-of-heaven.

2. **Tammuz.** Ezekiel sees women 'weeping for Tammuz' at the north gate of the temple (Ezek 8:14). Tammuz is Ishtar's lover Dumuzi, so the rite belongs to her cycle.

3. **Nineveh as a seductive woman.** Nahum calls Nineveh 'the well-favoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts' (Nah 3:4). Some interpreters hear an allusion to Ishtar of Nineveh, the city's great goddess; this is plausible but not provable.

4. **Esther's name.** Esther's Persian name is often derived from Ishtar; others derive it from Persian *stara*, 'star'. Since Ishtar was the star goddess, the two ideas overlap. Debated.
16043: Cakes for the Queen of Heaven
16044: Whole families in Judah, and later refugees in Egypt, honoured a goddess with cakes 'in her image'. The refugees told Jeremiah that things went well when they served her and badly when they stopped. Identification with Ishtar is likely in part, but debated.
16045: Ezekiel's vision of the temple shows women mourning Ishtar's dying lover — a rite from her mythology practised at the house of Yahweh.
16047: Nahum's portrait of Nineveh as a seductive sorceress may borrow imagery from the city's goddess.
